extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and educated readers interested in geophysics, terrestrial magnetism, and physical geography
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical principles for measuring and interpreting the Earth's internal structure, heat distribution, and magnetic phenomena, aimed at readers conducting or evaluating geophysical observations and hypotheses. Covers recommended measurements, typical numerical benchmarks, sources of error, and limits of analytic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum as a geognostical instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The vertical as well as the horizontally vibrating pendulum may justly be termed a geognostical instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendulum experiments (vertical and horizontal) can be used to infer mean density and internal compression of the Earth; results (e.g., Reich) guide hypotheses about increasing density toward the center. Use pendulum measurements alongside mineralogical density estimates of surface strata to infer interior density gradients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean density benchmarks and inference about interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Reich's experiments give a mean density of the whole Earth of 5.44 times that of pure water; continental dry strata ~2.7, dry+liquid surface conjointly ~1.6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare measured global mean density (~5.44) with surface-strata densities to infer that interior layers must greatly increase in density toward the center (due to pressure and/or heterogeneous composition). Use these numerical benchmarks when evaluating models of Earth's interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward arbitrary/venturous internal models
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectures such as a hollow sphere nucleus filled with 'imponderable matter' or fanciful populated inner worlds conflict with compression limits and established natural laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject speculative internal-world models that ignore measured compression and densities; ensure hypotheses are consistent with physical constraints (e.g., compression calculations) and observed data rather than imaginative extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution applying idealized analytic heat-motion models
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic calculations of heat motion in homogeneous metallic spheroids (Fourier and similar) must be applied with much caution to the actual Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for Earth's heterogeneous composition, varying heat capacities and conductivities of superimposed masses, and chemical/physical changes under compression. Use analytic models as guides but not definitive descriptions; note Poisson's alternative hypotheses and limitations of homogenous assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of borehole/mine temperature measurements for geothermal gradient
rubrics_metrics.description: Artesian wells and mine temperature measurements show an increase of terrestrial heat with depth (various reported gradients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical empirical results: Arago/Puits de Grenelle and similar: ~1 degree per ~51.8 feet; Reich: ~1 degree per 76.3 feet; Phillips/Monk-wearmouth: ~1 degree per 59.06 feet. When estimating depth-to-melting or geothermal gradients, use multiple borehole measurements and recognize variability across sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for measurement errors in boreholes/mines
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arise from lateral permeation of water and from currents of cold air commonly present in mines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting borehole temperatures, correct for lateral water flows and ventilation/cold air currents; prefer comparative results from several independent bores (different depths and locations) to mitigate local errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of heat transmission in the globe
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish periodic (seasonal penetration from surface), slow equator-to-pole internal transfer, and the slowest — secular cooling of the globe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to interpret different temporal/spatial temperature signals: short-period surface-driven oscillations, long-term internal redistribution, and secular cooling from primordial heat. Recognize which mode dominates for the phenomenon under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of astronomical/geodetic measures for long-term thermal stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of secular inequalities in lunar motion and ancient eclipses indicates the length of the day has not diminished appreciably in ~2000 years, constraining Earth's mean temperature change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ changes (or invariance) in Earth's rotatory velocity (length of day) over millennia as constraints on secular changes of Earth's mean internal heat. Example bound: length of day not diminished by 1/100 second in 2000 years implies a temperature decrease <1/306th degree Fahrenheit under certain material-dilation assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of hydraulic laws for semi-fluid deep strata
rubrics_metrics.description: Known laws of hydraulics apply only under considerable modification to semi-fluid or semi-solid deep-earth substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid naively applying surface hydraulics to interpret subterranean semi-fluid behavior; expect modifications due to extreme pressures, variable rheology, and complex boundary conditions between molten and solid layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifestations of terrestrial magnetism classified into three phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnetic phenomena on the surface manifest as variation in intensity, variation in inclination, and horizontal deviation (declination) from the terrestrial meridian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent these manifestations by isodynamic (equal force), isoclinic (equal inclination), and isogonic (equal declination) lines. Use the three systems together when mapping and interpreting terrestrial magnetism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnetic storms: simultaneity and locality considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnetic storms can manifest simultaneously over vast regions, but local perturbations exist that do not extend far (example: Freiberg mines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using magnetic storms as phenomena (e.g., for longitude determination), verify simultaneity across stations and be alert to local disturbances that may invalidate regional inferences. Historical examples (25 Sept 1841) show near-global simultaneity; other rare local events affect only small areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using magnetic inclination for latitude determination (local application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Between certain coastal latitudinal arrangements, the inclination of the magnetic needle can determine whether a ship is north or south of a port independently of time or celestial observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply magnetic-inclination methods where isoclinic lines change predictably along a north–south coast (e.g., parts of Chili and Peru). Recognize method's limited geographic applicability (local) and that it fails where isoclinic lines run parallel to the coast or change irregularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and origins of magnetism: permanent vs induced
rubrics_metrics.description: Iron and nickel (probably cobalt) are the substances that become permanently magnetic and retain polarity under a coercive force; many substances can be transiently magnetic when conducting currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing magnetic properties to samples, test purity (impurities like nickel can confer magnetism), and distinguish permanent magnetism from transient induced effects (e.g., Arago and Faraday's experiments showing conduction-induced magnetism). Be cautious about historical misidentifications (e.g., chrome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diurnal (horary) variation patterns and dependence on magnetic latitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Horary variations (daily) of declination are governed by the Sun while above the horizon and diminish in angular value with magnetic latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect larger daily declination oscillations in mid-latitudes (13–14 minutes in middle Europe) and much smaller near equator (3–4 minutes). Recognize that northern and southern hemispheres show opposite senses of daily motion; this implies there is a region between terrestrial and magnetic equators with negligible horary deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secular motion of isogonic/isoclinic/isodynamic lines and chart comparison limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Isogonic lines advance and become inflected when passing from sea to continent; their secular motion means graphical representations from different centuries may not be directly comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing magnetic charts across time, account for secular progression and land/ocean-induced inflection of magnetic curves. Do not assume stationarity; historical maps must be interpreted in light of secular changes and local influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local invariability vs regional secular change in declination
rubrics_metrics.description: Some locations show little or no change in magnetic declination over centuries (e.g., parts of the Antilles, Spitzbergen), whereas other regions (e.g., England) have experienced substantial secular drift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check local historical declination records before assuming constancy; survey and cadastral work relying on the compass must account for possible secular drift or long-term local invariability to avoid land-measurement errors.
